Two new species of a small, brightly coloured butterfly from Madagascar have been described by researchers at The Natural History Museum.
The two newly discovered butterflies are members of one of only three genera in their family and were found on an expedition to central western Madagascar. They belong to the subfamily Satyrinae which is part of the larger group known as brush-footed or longwing butterflies (Nymphalidae).
They join 11 other recently-described Madagascan satyrids including several previously unknown species that had not even yet received scientific names until now.
Dr David Newland , Research Associate Curator Entomology said: “These beautiful little creatures really do look like they’ve stepped out straight off some tropical island.”
“Madagascar has such high levels of endemism – meaning it’s home to many unique animals - but this particular area was relatively unexplored so we’re very excited about these discoveries,” he added
Both species can be distinguished based upon colouration; Pseudonacaduba madagascariensis being predominantly black with white spots while its relative Pseudonacidina malaheloana features bright red markings across both wings.

Two new species of a small, brightly coloured butterfly from Madagascar have been described by researchers at The Natural History Museum.
The two newly discovered butterflies are members of one of only three genera in their family and were found on an expedition to central western Madagascar. They belong to the subfamily Satyrinae which is part of the larger group known as brush-footed or longwing butterflies (Nymphalidae).
They join 11 other recently-described Madagascan satyrids including several previously unknown species that had not even yet received scientific names until now.
Dr David Newland , Research Associate Curator Entomology said: “These beautiful little creatures really do look like they’ve stepped out straight off some tropical island.”
“Madagascar has such high levels of endemism – meaning it’s home to many unique animals - but this particular area was relatively unexplored so we’re very excited about these discoveries,” he added
Both species can be distinguished based upon colouration; Pseudonacaduba madagascariensis being predominantly black with white spots while its relative Pseudonacidina malaheloana features bright red markings across both wings.

Two new species of a small, brightly coloured butterfly from Madagascar have been described by researchers at The Natural History Museum.
The two newly discovered butterflies are members of one of only three genera in their family and were found on an expedition to central western Madagascar. They belong to the subfamily Satyrinae which is part of the larger group known as brush-footed or longwing butterflies (Nymphalidae).
They join 11 other recently-described Madagascan satyrids including several previously unknown species that had not even yet received scientific names until now.
Dr David Newland , Research Associate Curator Entomology said: “These beautiful little creatures really do look like they’ve stepped out straight off some tropical island.”
“Madagascar has such high levels of endemism – meaning it’s home to many unique animals - but this particular area was relatively unexplored so we’re very excited about these discoveries,” he added
Both species can be distinguished based upon colouration; Pseudonacaduba madagascariensis being predominantly black with white spots while its relative Pseudonacidina malaheloana features bright red markings across both wings.
Pseudonacada madagascarensis : A male specimen photographed during fieldwork in Western Central Madagascar © Dr D J W Newlands & M R Hanks / NHMUK

[ANS] A Baby Panda Goes To The Zoo - 2018-08-09, 11:00 AM (This post was last modified: 2020-01-06, 10:02 PM by ANS.)
A new-born giant panda cub has been taken from its mother and put on display at a Chinese wildlife park.
The animal is being kept in an enclosure with other pandas as part of efforts to boost breeding numbers. It will be fed milk every two hours for three months before it can join its parents again.
Giant Pandas are listed as "vulnerable" under international conservation laws because their population continues to decline due to habitat loss and poaching.
They live mainly in Sichuan province but also inhabit parts of Shaanxi and Gansu provinces.
Pandas have become one of China's most famous animals since they were first discovered more than a century ago.
In recent years there had only ever been about 1,800 left in the wild according to official figures released earlier this year.
But that number could now rise if all goes well after cubs born over the past few weeks start growing up together.
There are currently around 300 captive-bred babies living across zoos worldwide including Chengdu Research Base Of Giant Panda Breeding where the latest arrival lives.
It joins another recently hatched female which arrived just days later along with her brother who came into the world back in May.
All three youngsters come from different mothers so should not compete against each other when looking for mates once old enough.
Their father Xing Hui died aged nine-years-old while he lived out his life alongside five females at the base near Mount Qingcheng National Park.
He became known locally as Mr Happy after spending much time playing with visitors during public events held throughout the day.
His death prompted calls among some locals for him to receive state funeral honours similar those given to former President Jiang Zemin following his passing away late last month.
However officials said no such ceremony would take place despite requests made online through social media platforms like Weibo.
Instead staff members paid tribute to him inside the facility saying goodbye via video message played outside the entrance gates.
